section.name: Listen queues
section.para:
After the connection has been established it is placed in the listen queue of the listen socket. To see the current listen queues state, you may run the command “netstat -Lan”:
Current listen queue sizes (qlen/incqlen/maxqlen) Proto Listen Local Address tcp4 10/0/128 *.80 tcp4 0/0/128 *.22
This is a normal case: the listen queue of the port *:80 contains just 10 unaccepted connections. If the web server is not able to handle the load, you may see something like this:
Current listen queue sizes (qlen/incqlen/maxqlen) Proto Listen Local Address tcp4 192/0/128 *.80 tcp4 0/0/128 *.22
Here are 192 unaccepted connections and most likely new coming connections are discarding. Although the limit is 128 connections, FreeBSD allows receiving 1.5 times connections than the limit before it starts to discard the new connections. You may increase the limit using
sysctl kern.ipc.soacceptqueue=4096
However, note that the queue is only a damper to quench bursts. If it is always overflowed, this means that you need to improve the web server, but not to continue to increase the limit. You may also change the listen queue maximum size in nginx configuration:
listen 80 backlog=1024;
However, you may not set it more than the current kern.ipc.soacceptqueue value. By default nginx uses the maximum value of FreeBSD kernel.

section.name: Socket buffers
section.para: When a client sends a data, the data first is received by the kernel which places the data in the socket receiving buffer. Then an application such as the web server may call recv or read system calls to get the data from the buffer. When the application wants to send a data, it calls send or write system calls to place the data in the socket sending buffer. Then the kernel manages to send the data from the buffer to the client.

The initial sizes of the socket receiving and sending buffers are 64K and 32K respectively, and are set by the sysctls net.inet.tcp.recvspace and net.inet.tcp.sendspace. Then the kernel automatically grows the buffers of each connection as needed, up to the net.inet.tcp.recvbuf_max and net.inet.tcp.sendbuf_max values (8M by default). The sending buffer grows in net.inet.tcp.sendbuf_inc steps only when it is nearly full and the client is able to accept more data, so the buffers of slow clients stay small, while fast clients may use bigger TCP window sizes and obtain higher throughput. Therefore there is no need to increase the initial buffer sizes.

Note that the buffers are not shrunk back on idle connections. If there are a lot of simultaneous connections and memory is scarce, the maximum amount of memory devoted to one connection can be limited by decreasing the net.inet.tcp.sendbuf_max and net.inet.tcp.recvbuf_max values.

Setting buffer sizes explicitly with the sndbuf and rcvbuf parameters of the directive disables automatic sizing of the corresponding buffer for all connections accepted on the listen socket. Since nginx uses non-blocking I/O system calls and does not require large buffers to serve a lot of connections, these parameters are usually not needed.

section.name: mbufs, mbuf clusters, etc.
section.para: Inside the kernel the buffers are stored in the form of chains of memory chunks linked using the mbuf structures. The mbuf size is 256 bytes and it can be used to store a small amount of data, for example, TCP/IP header. However, the mbufs point mostly to other data stored in the mbuf clusters or jumbo clusters, or directly to physical memory pages (unmapped mbufs), and in this kind they are used as the chain links only. The mbuf cluster size is 2K. The jumbo cluster size can be equal to a CPU page size (4K for amd64), 9K, or 16K. The 9K and 16K jumbo clusters are used mainly in local networks with Ethernet frames larger than usual 1500 bytes, and they are beyond the scope of this article.

The limits of the mbufs and clusters are calculated at boot time from the amount of physical memory. The total memory available for mbufs and clusters, kern.ipc.maxmbufmem, is a half of physical memory by default. The kern.ipc.nmbclusters and kern.ipc.nmbjumbop limits are calculated so that the mbuf clusters and the page size jumbo clusters each may take a quarter of this memory. For example, on a system with 16G of physical memory, this gives about one million mbuf clusters and about half a million page size jumbo clusters. Note that these are only limits: the memory is allocated on demand. These defaults are sufficient for most workloads.

To see the current usage of the mbufs and clusters and their limits, you may run the command “netstat -m”. The lines to watch are:
0/0/0 requests for mbufs denied (mbufs/clusters/mbuf+clusters) 0/0/0 requests for jumbo clusters denied (4k/9k/16k)
Non-zero values there, as well as “kern.ipc.nmbclusters limit reached” and similar messages in the kernel log, mean that the limits were exhausted. In this case the limits can be increased on the fly, for example:
sysctl kern.ipc.nmbclusters=2000000 sysctl kern.ipc.nmbjumbop=1000000
The values cannot be decreased at runtime, and an attempt to set a value lower than the current one fails. The overall kern.ipc.maxmbufmem limit can be changed only at boot time in /boot/loader.conf, and it cannot exceed 3/4 of physical memory.

section.name: sendfile
section.para: The sendfile system call allows sending a file or its part to a socket directly without reading the parts in an application buffer. It is enabled in nginx with the directive. The sendfile passes to the TCP/IP stack the file pages that are already present in FreeBSD cache memory, without copying them. Thus, sendfile decreases both CPU usage by omitting two memory copy operations, and memory usage by using the cached file pages instead of mbuf clusters and jumbo clusters.

On platforms with a direct map of physical memory, such as amd64 and arm64, sendfile uses unmapped mbufs: each such mbuf points directly to several file pages (up to 5 pages on 64-bit platforms), so that fewer mbufs are needed and the pages need not be mapped into the kernel address space. This is controlled by the kern.ipc.mb_use_ext_pgs sysctl, which is enabled by default on these platforms. For the same reason the sf_bufs mappings are not used on these platforms, and need no tuning.

When sending files from the UFS file system, sendfile does not block on disk I/O: if file pages are not in memory, it starts reading them asynchronously and queues them in the socket sending buffer as not yet ready data, which are sent as soon as the read completes. Note that this does not apply to ZFS: it caches file data in its own cache (ARC), the file pages are filled from it, and sendfile blocks while uncached data are read from disk. The sendfile statistics can be seen in the “netstat -m” output.

To read file pages, sendfile uses a pool of physical buffers of the vnode pager. If the pool is exhausted, sendfile blocks, and the process is seen in the “zonelimit” state. The pool size can be increased with the vm.vnode_pbufs tunable in /boot/loader.conf.

The kernel TLS (kTLS) allows using sendfile for SSL connections as well: the data are encrypted by the kernel when sending, which also requires unmapped mbufs. The kTLS support is included in the default kernel configuration (options KERN_TLS) and is enabled by the kern.ipc.tls.enable sysctl, which is on by default. In nginx, kTLS is used with OpenSSL 3.0 or newer built with kTLS support (the base system OpenSSL on amd64 and arm64 is built so by default), when enabled with the directive:
ssl_conf_command Options KTLS;

section.name: Outgoing connections
section.para: Each outgoing connection, such as to a proxied server, uses a local port automatically chosen from the range of net.inet.ip.portrange.first to net.inet.ip.portrange.last, 10000–65535 by default. The same local port can be used simultaneously for connections to different addresses and ports, thus the range limits the number of connections to the same proxied server. The connections closed by nginx are kept in the TIME_WAIT state for 2 × net.inet.tcp.msl (60 seconds by default) and keep using their ports. For connections to local addresses, the net.inet.tcp.msl_local value is used instead, 10 milliseconds by default.

The preferred way to reduce the number of the outgoing connections is to use keepalive connections to proxied servers. Otherwise, the range can be extended:
net.inet.ip.portrange.first=1024 net.inet.ip.portrange.last=65535
Note that in this case the ports may clash with ports of other services listening on the same addresses. Other ways are to use several proxied server addresses or ports, or several local addresses with the directive.

By default, the local port is chosen randomly. At high rates of outgoing connections, sequential port allocation can be used instead, so that each port is reused as late as possible:
net.inet.ip.portrange.randomized=0
Note that this makes local ports predictable, and thus makes spoofing attacks easier.

section.name: Finalizing connection
section.para:
When nginx closes a connection, the connection moves to the FIN_WAIT_2 state after the client acknowledges the closing, and stays there until the client closes the connection on its side. If the client never does this, for example, if it has disappeared, the connection is kept until it is idle for net.inet.tcp.keepcnt × net.inet.tcp.keepintvl, that is 10 minutes by default. The following setting allows dropping such connections after the net.inet.tcp.finwait2_timeout (60 seconds by default):
net.inet.tcp.fast_finwait2_recycle=1
